title: A natural nuclear reactor ran in Gabon 1.7 billion years ago
body: In May 1972, routine checks at a French uranium enrichment plant found ore from the Oklo mine in Gabon with only 0.60% uranium-235 instead of the usual 0.72%. Something had already ‘burned’ part of it. Billions of years ago natural uranium was richer, about 3.1% U-235, enough to sustain fission once groundwater seeped in and slowed the neutrons. The deposit ran as a **natural reactor** for a few hundred thousand years, in pulses of about 30 minutes of fission followed by about two and a half hours of cooling, never above 100 kilowatts of heat. Sixteen such reactor zones have been found.

slides.heading: How rock went critical
items: 1.7 billion years ago, uranium ore at Oklo, in Gabon, held about 3.1% uranium-235
Groundwater seeping in slowed the neutrons enough to sustain a chain reaction
Heat boiled the water away, stopping the reaction; it cooled, water returned, and it restarted

slides.label: uranium-235 in the Oklo ore, instead of the usual 0.72%
slides.text: The missing fraction had been split by fission long ago. Later samples ran as low as 0.44%.

slides.heading: Uranium-235 as a share of natural uranium
slides.note: U-235 decays faster than U-238, so its share keeps falling; fission cut Oklo’s further.

left.label: On
left.text: About 30 minutes of fission, heating the rock and boiling off the water.

right.label: Off
right.text: About 2.5 hours of cooling until water seeps back and the reaction restarts.

slides.question: Why can’t a reactor like Oklo start up in uranium ore today?
options: Natural uranium is now too lean
slides.explanation: Uranium-235 decays faster than uranium-238, so natural uranium has fallen from about 3.1% U-235 to 0.72%, too little for water-moderated rock to go critical.
